title: 46. Numeracy & Number Systems: Determining a Whole from a Percentage
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Determining a Whole from a Percentage
questions.learningObjective: Determine a whole quantity when a simple percentage of the whole is known.
questions.question: \(20\%\) of a number is \(14\). What is the number?
questions.explanation: Let the whole number be \(x\). Since \(20\%\) of \(x\) is \(14\), \(0.20x=14\). Divide by \(0.20\): \(x=14\div0.20=70\). Therefore, the whole number is \(70\).
questions.hint: Divide the known percentage amount by the percentage written as a decimal.

questions.concept: Determining a Whole from a Fractional Percentage
questions.learningObjective: Determine a whole quantity when one quarter of the whole is known.
questions.question: \(25\%\) of a number is \(18\). What is the number?
questions.explanation: Since \(25\%=\frac{1}{4}\), the known amount \(18\) is one quarter of the whole. Therefore, the whole is \(18\times4=72\).
questions.hint: Express \(25\%\) as a simple fraction and use the relationship between the part and the whole.

questions.concept: Determining a Whole from a Known Percentage Amount
questions.learningObjective: Use division by a decimal percentage to determine an unknown whole.
questions.question: \(40\%\) of a number is \(36\). What is the number?
questions.explanation: Let the whole be \(x\). Then \(0.40x=36\). Dividing both sides by \(0.40\) gives \(x=36\div0.40=90\). Therefore, the whole is \(90\).
questions.hint: The known amount equals the decimal form of the percentage multiplied by the whole.

questions.concept: Determining a Whole from a Decimal Percentage
questions.learningObjective: Determine a whole quantity from a known amount representing a decimal percentage of the whole.
questions.question: \(12.5\%\) of a number is \(11\). What is the number?
questions.explanation: \(12.5\%=\frac{1}{8}\). If \(\frac{1}{8}\) of the whole is \(11\), then the whole is \(11\times8=88\). Therefore, the number is \(88\).
questions.hint: Convert \(12.5\%\) to a familiar fraction before determining the whole.

questions.concept: Recovering a Whole from a Percentage
questions.learningObjective: Recover an unknown whole by dividing a known percentage amount by its decimal rate.
questions.question: \(60\%\) of a quantity is \(42\). What is the whole quantity?
questions.explanation: Let the whole quantity be \(x\). Then \(0.60x=42\). Therefore, \(x=42\div0.60=70\). The whole quantity is \(70\).
questions.hint: Do not calculate the percentage of \(42\). Instead, use \(42\) as the known percentage amount and work backward to the whole.

questions.concept: Determining a Whole from a Small Decimal Percentage
questions.learningObjective: Determine a whole when a small decimal percentage of it is known.
questions.question: \(7.5\%\) of a quantity is \(18\). What is the whole quantity?
questions.explanation: Convert \(7.5\%\) to \(0.075\). If the whole is \(x\), then \(0.075x=18\). Thus, \(x=18\div0.075=240\). Therefore, the whole quantity is \(240\).
questions.hint: Convert \(7.5\%\) to a decimal, then divide the known part by that decimal.

questions.concept: Determining a Whole from a Percentage Greater Than 100
questions.learningObjective: Determine an original whole when a known quantity represents more than 100 percent of it.
questions.question: \(120\%\) of a number is \(54\). What is the number?
questions.explanation: \(120\%=1.20\). Let the original number be \(x\). Then \(1.20x=54\), so \(x=54\div1.20=45\). Therefore, the original number is \(45\).
questions.hint: Write \(120\%\) as a decimal; the known amount equals that decimal multiplied by the number, so divide to recover the number.

questions.concept: Determining a Total from a Percentage Count
questions.learningObjective: Determine a total number of objects when a percentage and its corresponding count are known.
questions.question: In a school activity, \(35\%\) of the participating students are in Group A. If Group A has \(84\) students, how many students are participating altogether?
questions.explanation: Let the total number of participating students be \(x\). Since \(35\%\) of them equals \(84\), \(0.35x=84\). Therefore, \(x=84\div0.35=240\). There are \(240\) participating students altogether.
questions.hint: Treat the group count as the known percentage amount and work backward to the total.

questions.concept: Determining an Original Whole from the Remaining Percentage
questions.learningObjective: Determine an original whole by first identifying the percentage represented by a remaining quantity.
questions.question: After \(20\%\) of a supply is used, \(144\) units remain. How many units were in the original supply?
questions.explanation: If \(20\%\) is used, then \(100\%-20\%=80\%\) remains. Thus, \(80\%\) of the original supply is \(144\). Let the original supply be \(x\). Then \(0.80x=144\), so \(x=144\div0.80=180\). Therefore, the original supply contained \(180\) units.
questions.hint: First determine what percentage of the original supply remains, then use the remaining amount to recover the whole.

questions.concept: Determining a Whole from Successive Percentages
questions.learningObjective: Determine an original whole from a known amount produced by two successive percentage relationships.
questions.question: In a library, \(30\%\) of all books are science books. Of the science books, \(40\%\) are currently borrowed. If \(36\) science books are currently borrowed, how many books are in the library altogether?
questions.explanation: The \(36\) borrowed science books represent \(40\%\) of all science books. Therefore, the number of science books is \(36\div0.40=90\). These \(90\) science books represent \(30\%\) of all books. Thus, the total number of books is \(90\div0.30=300\). Therefore, the library has \(300\) books altogether.
questions.hint: Work backward in two stages: first recover the total number of science books, then use that result to recover the total number of books.
